379.title: The basket in the reeds (Exodus 2:1–10)
379.hook: a mother, a sister watching, a princess who pities a crying baby
379.howItsDone: Christians tell the story of baby Moses to children, and some read it alongside Matthew 2, where the infant Jesus escapes King Herod; churches use it to speak about protecting children and welcoming adopted and foster children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the midwives: Shiphrah and Puah feared God more than Pharaoh. Your line was two women said no.

When the midwives won't do it, Pharaoh stops pretending. He orders all his people: every son born to the Hebrews, throw him into the river. Into this, a baby boy is born to a family from the tribe of Levi. His mother sees, the text says, that he is a goodly child, and she hides him for three months. Three months of a newborn, hidden: the crying, the night feedings, the neighbors. Then he gets too big and too loud to hide.
screen: `THROW THEM IN THE RIVER.` → `A GOODLY CHILD.` → `HIDDEN THREE MONTHS.`

segments.voice: So she does something brave and strange. In the King James Bible: "she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink." An ark. The Hebrew word is tevah, the same word Genesis uses for Noah's ark: once a boat that carried the whole world through the flood, now a little one, sealed with tar, carrying one baby. She puts him in the very river Pharaoh wanted him thrown into. "And his sister stood afar off, to wit what would be done to him." Someone was watching. Then Pharaoh's daughter comes down to bathe. She has the basket brought and opens it, "and, behold, the babe wept. And she had compassion on him." She knows he's one of the Hebrews' children, and she keeps him anyway, against her own father's order. Now the sister moves: shall I find a Hebrew woman to nurse him for you? Go, says the princess. So the sister brings back the baby's own mother, who is paid to nurse her own son. When he's older, the princess adopts him and names him: "Because I drew him out of the water." Moses. Look at who saves him: a mother, a sister, a foreign princess, and before them, two midwives. Not one of them is a king or a soldier, and the one with royal blood is defying her own father. Every one of them was paying attention. Some Christian readers notice another baby, in Matthew's Gospel, whose life was threatened by a king, carried to safety in Egypt.

380.title: Moses runs (Exodus 2:11–22)
380.hook: he kills an Egyptian, flees, and becomes a stranger in a strange land
380.carry: a stranger in a strange land
380.howItsDone: Christians often draw on Moses's years as a stranger in Midian, and on the laws about strangers that follow from Israel's time in Egypt, when churches welcome immigrants and refugees.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tevah: a mother, a sister, a princess, and a baby drawn out of the water. Your line was someone was watching.

Moses grows up in the palace: Egyptian clothes, Egyptian schooling, a princess for a mother. But he knows, somehow, who his people are. One day, a grown man, he goes out and watches them carrying their loads. He sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own. Moses looks this way and that way, sees no one, kills the Egyptian, and hides the body in the sand. It's the first thing the adult Moses does in the Bible. Not a miracle. A killing, done in anger, in secret, with a glance over his shoulder.
screen: `RAISED IN THE PALACE.` → `HE SEES THE BEATING.` → `THIS WAY AND THAT WAY.`

segments.voice: The next day he sees two Hebrews fighting, and tells the one in the wrong to stop. The man turns on him, in the King James Bible: "Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?" Are you going to kill me like you killed the Egyptian? So it's known. Pharaoh wants him dead, and Moses runs, east out of Egypt, all the way to the land of Midian, and sits down by a well. Wells keep turning up in this story: Rebekah at one, Jacob and Rachel at another. Seven sisters come to water their father's flock, and shepherds drive them off. Moses stands up for them and waters their flock. At home they tell their father: an Egyptian rescued us. In Egypt he's a Hebrew. In Midian he's an Egyptian. He belongs nowhere. The father takes him in, Moses marries one of the daughters, Zipporah, and they have a son. Moses names him Gershom, saying: "I have been a stranger in a strange land." Ger is the Hebrew word for a stranger, a foreigner living among people not their own. Christians and Jews have both struggled with the killing: was it justice, or rage? In the book of Acts, Stephen retells it as Moses taking his people's side, supposing they would understand that God meant to free them by his hand; they didn't. The Bible doesn't settle it. But it never forgets what Moses learned in Midian. Israel's law will later say: don't oppress a stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.

Now think of someone around you who is new right now, a neighbor, a coworker, a family at school, and picture greeting them. If you pray, you can pray for them.

381.title: The burning bush (Exodus 3:1–6)
381.hook: a bush on fire and not burned up: take off your shoes, this is holy ground
381.howItsDone: In Ethiopian Orthodox churches and some other Christian communities, worshippers remove their shoes before entering, and Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor an icon of the Unburnt Bush linked to Mary; Christians also read Exodus 3 as a call to notice God in ordinary places.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses ran to Midian and named his son for what he'd become. Your line was a stranger in a strange land.

Years pass, in process of time, as the King James text says. The king of Egypt dies, the Israelites groan under their slavery and cry out, and God hears. Moses doesn't know any of that. He's a shepherd now, keeping his father-in-law Jethro's sheep deep in the wilderness, near a mountain called Horeb. A former prince, walking behind sheep in the heat. An ordinary workday: no temple, no altar, no warning. Then, out of the corner of his eye, a bush is on fire.
screen: `GOD HEARS THE CRY.` → `MOSES THE SHEPHERD.` → `A BUSH ON FIRE.`

segments.voice: Bushes catch fire in the desert. What's strange is this, in the King James Bible: "the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed." It burns, and it doesn't burn up. Moses says, "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt." That small choice matters. When the Lord saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him from the middle of the bush: "Moses, Moses." And Moses answers with the words Abraham and Jacob said before him: "Here am I." Then: don't come any closer. "Put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." It's the same dirt he walked on yesterday with the sheep. What makes it holy is who is there. God names himself, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, of Jacob, and Moses hides his face, afraid to look. Christians have seen many things in this bush. In Orthodox and Catholic tradition, a bush that holds fire without burning up became a picture of Mary, who carried God within her. In Ethiopian Orthodox churches, worshippers take off their shoes before they enter. And the English poet Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote: "Earth's crammed with heaven, and every common bush afire with God; but only he who sees, takes off his shoes." The fire was there. Moses turned aside.

382.title: I AM (Exodus 3:13–15)
382.hook: asked his name, God answers I AM THAT I AM
382.howItsDone: The King James Bible, like many English Bibles, prints the divine name as LORD in small capitals, following the Jewish practice of not pronouncing it, and Christians read the "I am" sayings in John's Gospel alongside Exodus 3:14.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seneh: a fire that didn't burn up, and bare feet on holy ground. Your line was holy ground.

At the bush, God gives Moses a job: go back to Egypt and bring my people out. Moses has questions. The first is: who am I, to go to Pharaoh? The second is sharper. Suppose the Israelites ask, what is his name? What do I tell them? Jacob asked it too, after wrestling all night by the river: "Tell me, I pray thee, thy name." He got a blessing instead of an answer. Moses wants something to say. What he gets is not a name like any other.
screen: `GO BACK TO EGYPT.` → `WHO AM I?` → `WHAT IS HIS NAME?`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you." In Hebrew it's three words: ehyeh asher ehyeh. Ehyeh comes from the verb to be. It can mean I am who I am, or I will be what I will be. Scholars still argue, and the honest answer is that the Hebrew holds both. A name that won't sit still: not a statue you can carry, not a label you can control. Then God adds the name Israel will use, four Hebrew letters, Y, H, W, H, closely related to that verb to be. "This is my name for ever, and this is my memorial unto all generations." Out of reverence, Jews stopped saying it aloud long ago. When they read it, they say Adonai, my Lord, or call it simply HaShem, the Name. The King James Bible follows a similar path: wherever you see LORD in small capital letters, that's this name. The English word Jehovah came later, from combining the four letters with the vowels of Adonai. How it was first pronounced, nobody knows for certain. Christians hear this name again in the Gospel of John, where Jesus says, "Before Abraham was, I am." Christian tradition hears in it the name from the bush. So God doesn't give Moses a title. God gives him a verb: I am. I will be.

383.title: Moses' excuses (Exodus 4:10–17)
383.hook: I'm slow of speech; send someone else, please
383.carry: I will be with your mouth
383.howItsDone: Christians return to Moses's excuses when they feel called to something and unready for it, and Exodus 4 is preached to people nervous about speaking, teaching or serving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a name that is a verb: I am that I am, four letters printed LORD. Your line was I am that I am.

Reasons not to are easy to find. I'm not qualified. I'm not ready. Someone else would be better at this. At the burning bush, Moses runs through the whole list. First: who am I, to go to Pharaoh? God says, I will be with you. Second: what's your name? God answers, I AM. Third: what if they don't believe me? God gives him signs, a staff that turns into a snake, a hand that turns white and back. A talking fire, a new name for God, miracles on demand. But Moses has two more excuses left.
screen: `WHO AM I?` → `WHAT IS YOUR NAME?` → `THEY WON'T BELIEVE ME.`

segments.voice: The fourth, in the King James Bible: "O my Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue." In Hebrew, heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue. Nobody knows exactly what that means. Some readers think Moses had a stammer; some, that he'd lost his Egyptian after years in the desert. A later Jewish story tells of the baby Moses burning his tongue on a coal in Pharaoh's palace. The Bible itself just says heavy. God answers with a question: "Who hath made man's mouth?" Then today's line: "Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say." Not, I'll fix your mouth. I'll be with it. Then the fifth excuse, stripped of reasons: "O my Lord, send, I pray thee, by the hand of him whom thou wilt send." Send someone else. Please. Here, the text says, God's anger burns. And still God doesn't give up on him. Your brother Aaron can speak well, God says, and he's already on his way to meet you. He'll be your mouth, I'll be with both your mouths, and take the staff. So the reluctant one goes, with help. Paul writes that God chose the weak things of the world. Jeremiah protests that he is only a child; Isaiah, that his lips are unclean. The Bible's leaders keep beginning with I can't, and keep being told, I will be with you.

384.title: Let my people go (Exodus 5:1–9)
384.hook: Moses asks, and Pharaoh makes them gather their own straw
384.howItsDone: In Black churches in America, the Exodus story and the spiritual Go Down, Moses have shaped preaching on freedom and justice, and Christians read the chapter when praying for people who are oppressed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five excuses at the bush, and one answer. Your line was I will be with your mouth.

Four words have traveled a long way from this chapter. Enslaved people in America sang them in a spiritual called Go Down, Moses. Harriet Tubman, who led people out of slavery, was called Moses. Preachers in the civil rights movement thundered them from pulpits. Let my people go. It sounds like a victory. But the first time the words are spoken in the Bible, they don't work at all. In fact, they make everything worse.
screen: `GO DOWN, MOSES.` → `HARRIET TUBMAN.` → `THE FIRST TIME, IT FAILS.`

segments.voice: Moses and Aaron, the reluctant speaker and his brother, walk in to the king of Egypt and say it, in the King James Bible: "Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Let my people go, that they may hold a feast unto me in the wilderness." Notice the request. Not, set them free forever. Just, let them go and worship. Pharaoh's answer starts the real contest: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go? I know not the LORD, neither will I let Israel go." Who is the Lord? Pharaoh is about to find out, but not yet. First he answers a request for relief by adding to the load. Until now, the slaves were given straw to mix into their bricks. Now: "Ye shall no more give the people straw to make brick, as heretofore: let them go and gather straw for themselves." Same number of bricks. Find your own straw. They're idle, he says; that's why they cry out about worship. The Israelite foremen are beaten when the bricks fall short. They turn on Moses and Aaron: you've made us stink in Pharaoh's eyes. And Moses, who didn't want this job, turns to God: why have you done this to your people? Why did you ever send me? The Bible keeps that complaint. It doesn't hide that doing the right thing can make things worse before they get better. Christians and Jews have both read this chapter as a picture of how oppression answers a request for freedom. The people who sang it later knew that. They sang it anyway.
screen: `LET THEM HOLD A FEAST TO ME.` · `WHO IS THE LORD?` · `NO STRAW, SAME BRICKS.` · `WHY DID YOU SEND ME?` · then, large: `LET MY PEOPLE GO.`

segments.voice: Think of someone being pushed down right now, a person you know, a group in the news, a worker whose load keeps growing, and picture them gathering straw in the dark. Then find one true sentence you could say for them, to someone who could help. If you pray, you can pray for them.

385.title: The plagues (Exodus 7–10)
385.hook: river to blood, frogs, darkness; Pharaoh hardens his heart again and again
385.howItsDone: Christians often preach on Pharaoh's hardened heart as a warning about repeated refusal, and churches differ on how they explain God hardening it; at the Passover Seder, Jews recite the plagues and spill a drop of wine for each.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharaoh, a king who answered a plea for worship by taking away the straw. Your line was who is the Lord?

Most people know the list, or most of it. The Nile turns to blood, and the fish die. Frogs everywhere: in the bedrooms, the ovens, the kneading bowls. Then lice. Swarms of flies. A sickness on the livestock. Boils on people and animals. Hail mixed with fire. Locusts that eat whatever the hail left. And then darkness so thick it could be felt, for three days. Nine disasters in four chapters. The movies make it a special-effects show. But read slowly, and the plagues aren't the main event. The main event is happening inside one man.
screen: `BLOOD, FROGS, LICE, FLIES.` → `HAIL, LOCUSTS, DARKNESS.` → `INSIDE ONE MAN.`

segments.voice: Watch Pharaoh. The frogs come, and he begs Moses: take them away, and I'll let the people go. The frogs die. Then, in the King James Bible: "when Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart, and hearkened not unto them." Relief, and he takes it back. Again and again. During the hail he even says, I have sinned this time; then the hail stops, and he changes his mind. After the lice, his own magicians tell him: "This is the finger of God." He won't hear it. The Hebrew uses three words for what happens to his heart: it becomes strong, hard, and heavy. Early on, the text says Pharaoh hardened his own heart, or that his heart was hardened. Later: "the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh." That has troubled readers for centuries, and Christians answer it differently. Some, drawing on Paul in Romans, stress that God is sovereign even over a king's will. Others notice that Pharaoh hardens first, many times, and read the later lines as God confirming the choice Pharaoh kept making. Both readings take the text seriously. And everyone notices the pattern: each no makes the next one easier. Look back over this week: a basket in the reeds, a stranger in Midian, a fire in a bush, I am that I am, five excuses, a request refused. One man said here am I. Another kept saying no. In the ninth plague, darkness covers Egypt, and the text adds one line: "all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings."
screen: `RESPITE, AND HE TAKES IT BACK.` · `THIS IS THE FINGER OF GOD.` · `STRONG, HARD, HEAVY.` · `WHO HARDENED WHOSE HEART?` · then, large: `A HARD HEART GETS HARDER.`

segments.voice: Think of a person or a subject where your no has become automatic: a relative, an old argument, a part of the news you've stopped feeling anything about. You don't have to change your mind; just feel the weight there, and ask whether it has grown. If you pray, you can ask for a softer heart; if you don't, simply let the weight be seen.
The plagues. The disasters that struck Egypt, from blood in the Nile to three days of darkness, while Pharaoh's heart grew harder each time.
Your line: a hard heart gets harder. It happens one small no at a time. That's day three hundred eighty-five.
